paragraph: Turning to Rama, Visvamitra said, "Behold the bow my son" and with his nod of approval, Rama took hold of the bow strung it, drew it and then the bow broke. The assembled multitude watched in awe and heard in fear that noise which was like a clap of thunder which reverberated from all directions. The earth shuddered as if the mountains were splitting. Of all those beholding the divine display of strength and valor, only Visvamithra, Janaka, and the two Raghavas remained standing while the rest, stunned, had fainted! The congregated masses slowly struggled back to their senses, seeming befuddled and dazed. When some semblance of normalcy had returned, king Janaka reverentially told Visvamitra that he had witnessed the strength of the great Ikshvaku prince, "I had pledged the hand of my daughter in marriage to him who would prove his might in handling the bow. I now bestow Sita on Rama, as a gift for that might". Sita with Rama as her lord will bring glory to my dynasty and she, who is dearer to me than my very life, shall be the consort of Rama. With your consent, my emissaries will hasten to Ayodhya to convey this news to Dasaratha'.
Chapter/Canto/Verse_Reference: Bala Kanda, Sarga 67 (Rama Breaks Siva's Bow)
Situation/Problem_Faced: Rama, with Visvamitra's approval, attempts to string Siva's mighty bow. In an incredible display of strength, Rama not only strings it but breaks it, causing a tremendous sound and tremor that stuns most observers. Janaka, recognizing Rama's unparalleled might, immediately declares his intention to marry Sita to Rama, fulfilling his long-standing pledge.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: This passage is a pivotal moment in the Ramayana, signifying Rama's extraordinary strength and divine power. It fulfills Janaka's condition for Sita's marriage, establishing the destined union. The widespread shock and awe highlight the magnitude of Rama's feat and his emerging heroic status. It also underscores Visvamitra's foresight and wisdom in bringing Rama to Mithila for this very purpose.
Outcome/Resolution: At Visvamitra's urging, Rama attempts to string Siva's bow. He successfully strings it, but in the process, breaks it with a thunderous sound that causes widespread shock and fainting among the onlookers. Janaka, deeply impressed by Rama's unmatched strength, pledges Sita's hand in marriage to him, fulfilling his vow. He then seeks Visvamitra's consent to send emissaries to Ayodhya to inform King Dasaratha.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Dharma (Righteousness - Janaka fulfilling his pledge for Sita's marriage)
Paurusha (Valor/Strength - Rama's display of unmatched power)
Karma (Action/Consequence - the immediate result of Rama's deed)
Shakti (Power - the divine power inherent in Rama and the bow)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Rama's breaking of Siva's bow is a powerful display of his 'Shakti' (divine power) and 'Paurusha' (valor), fulfilling Janaka's 'Dharma' (righteous pledge) and aligning with 'Daiva' (divine destiny) for Sita's marriage. The cosmic reverberations and the fainting of the multitude underscore the profound spiritual significance of this event, marking Rama's emergence as a divine hero. Visvamitra's calm observation signifies his role in guiding this spiritual alignment.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, Rama's incredible feat evokes a primal 'fear' and 'awe' in the onlookers, demonstrating the overwhelming impact of raw, superhuman strength. The widespread fainting indicates a complete psychological overload. Janaka experiences profound 'fulfillment' and validation as his challenging pledge is met by a truly exceptional individual, leading to immense 'satisfaction' and the psychological release of a long-held burden. This event solidifies Rama's perceived heroic status and the beginning of a fated union, with strong psychological implications for all involved.
